chapter: Buck and Bubbles: Nazarro and Bubbles
title: Bubbles challenges the Lunceford band and Stump the Band
summary: With Lunceford's orchestra on the bill, Bubbles dares each band member to repeat his steps, which Green thinks inspired Lunceford's record Stump the Band.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel

blocks.x: Yes. See, Mr. Bubbles -- Buck and Bubbles, one time when the Jimmy Lunceford Orchestra came up to New York City, and they were all in a show one time up there, and Buck and Bubbles I would say was always stopping the show. And they'd have to do these encores. But the people loved to hear Bubbles tap dance, you know. He got a taste of what happened to me down south. They'd say, "Dance, Bubbles, Dance," and they called his name and everything. And he would say something funny about his partner had run out of music or something, and he'd say, "I'll tell you, how would you like to see me challenge this band? I'll dance against their instruments." So the audience applauds, you see. So somebody in the band would jump up and say, "How can you do

that? What instrument are you going to play?" He'd say, "I'm standing on my instrument," you see, or something like that, and make people laugh. So he says, "All right," he says, "I'll play my instrument and you repeat after me, you try to repeat after me." So he would do a step, some kind of rhythm, you know. Then one of the guys, he'd look at him, you, you. "Well, which one of you? You heard it didn't you?" And the guy would jump up with his instrument and try to play what he heard, you see. And he would choose like every member of the band would have to do something, till they get to the drums, you know. Then he'd do one, and he said, "I'm doing this here, and everybody in the band go out to do this at the same time." And he'd do another step, you see. Sure enough, they'd get up and they'd play it together, and it would sound something, you know. And it gave Mr. Lunceford an idea, I'm quite sure, because the next thing that I know of, about three weeks after that, they had a record on the juke boxes by Jimmy Lunceford and Orchestra, and it was called, "Stump the Band," and I'm quite sure that Mr. Bubbles, Buck and Bubbles inspired them to compose this song, "Stump the Band," you know. It was an instrumental, a musical number, see. But it was quite a sensation, see. And then they were always favorites. They continued to be favorites and they still are. As you know, right to this day, Mr. Bubbles is a great -- he's a great favorite with the public, you know, on television or in movies,

or whatever, you see. He's always -- he's always loved, I would say. That's really what he deserves. So I'm trying to carry on, you know. Because him not being here, you know. He hasn't been active in quite some time. I think he's convalescing, got over it. You know, I think we called him long distance on the telephone, and we talked to him, and he said something about some muscle spasm or something in one of his legs. Who knows? You never know about John Bubbles.
